title: CBRNE I: HazMat Recognition, PPE & Decon
learningObjectives: Recognize CBRNE/HazMat clues and apply Step 1-2-3 Plus.
Read DOT placards, NFPA 704 diamonds, and the ERG color pages.
Match PPE levels A–D to tasks.
Run gross, mass, and technical decontamination — and know when dry beats wet.

summary.title: CBRNE: Know Which Letter
summary.content: Chemical, Biological, Radiological, Nuclear, Explosive. Explosives are by far the most common terrorist weapon; chemicals the most common HazMat call; biological events start silently (at clinics, days later); radiological events are mostly a fear-and-decon problem unless doses are huge. Your scene questions: Is it still releasing? Is it on people (contamination)? Can it spread person-to-person? What PPE do I need?

summary.title: Recognition & Step 1-2-3 Plus
summary.content: Clues: multiple casualties with similar symptoms and no trauma, unexplained odors/mists/clouds/oily liquids, dead animals or wilted vegetation, explosions with unusual smoke or little damage, placards/labels/containers, people fleeing from one point. STEP 1: one casualty, no obvious cause → approach with normal caution. STEP 2: two casualties → approach with caution, report, consider options. STEP 3: three or more → DO NOT APPROACH; withdraw, contain, report (METHANE), isolate. PLUS: tell exposed people to get out of the area, remove outer clothing, and decontaminate ('Remove, Remove, Remove').

summary.title: Reading the Labels
summary.content: DOT PLACARDS show hazard class 1–9 (1 explosives, 2 gases, 3 flammable liquids, 4 flammable solids, 5 oxidizers, 6 toxic/infectious, 7 radioactive, 8 corrosives, 9 miscellaneous) and a 4-digit UN/NA ID. The ERG: YELLOW pages = look up by ID number; BLUE = by material name; ORANGE = guide pages (hazards, PPE, first aid, evacuation); GREEN = initial isolation & protective action distances for toxic-inhalation hazards. NFPA 704 diamond (fixed facilities): BLUE = health, RED = flammability, YELLOW = instability/reactivity, WHITE = special (W = water-reactive, OX = oxidizer); 0 = minimal → 4 = severe.

summary.title: PPE Levels
summary.content: LEVEL A: SCBA + fully encapsulating vapor-tight suit — highest skin and respiratory protection, unknown/vapor hazards (HazMat entry teams). LEVEL B: SCBA + splash-protective suit — highest respiratory, less skin protection. LEVEL C: air-purifying respirator (APR/PAPR) + splash suit — known agent and concentration, enough oxygen; typical for decon teams and hospital decon. LEVEL D: work uniform, no respiratory protection — never in a contaminated area. EMS without HazMat training works in the COLD zone and receives patients AFTER decon.

summary.title: Decontamination
summary.content: The single most effective step: REMOVE CLOTHING — removes the large majority (often quoted ~80–90%) of external contamination. GROSS/emergency decon: immediate disrobe + flush for life-threatening exposure. MASS decon: disrobe → dry decon (blot/wipe exposed skin) for most exposures → wet decon (high-volume, low-pressure water, e.g., ladder-pipe/fire-engine corridor) for caustics, visible liquid contamination, or symptoms → re-dress/cover. TECHNICAL decon: thorough decon of responders/equipment. Ambulatory and non-ambulatory lanes; keep families together; give privacy and warmth; bag and tag belongings. Decon before transport — always. Life threats (airway, bleeding, antidotes) are managed in the warm zone by protected, trained providers during decon.

clinicalPearls: Three down, stay out: Step 1-2-3 is the rescuer's survival rule.
Clothing off is decon step one — and it's free, fast, and can be done by the patient.
Dry decon first for most exposures; go wet for caustics, visible liquid, or symptoms.
A contaminated patient in your ambulance takes the ambulance and crew out of service.
Expect many contaminated patients to self-present to hospitals — warn them early.
redFlags: Rescuers developing symptoms (eye irritation, cough, miosis) — withdraw and decon everyone.
Responders entering the hot zone in Level D.
Skipping decon because the patient is critical — do rapid gross decon with LSIs instead.
Treatment area downwind of the release.
commonMistakes: Confusing ERG yellow (ID number) and blue (name) pages.
Thinking Level C protects in oxygen-deficient or unknown atmospheres (it doesn't — it filters air).
Using high-pressure water or scrubbing that abrades skin.
Forgetting modesty, warmth, and family grouping in mass decon — people avoid decon and self-evacuate.
memoryAids: Step 1-2-3 Plus: 1 = approach, 2 = caution, 3 = don't approach + 'Remove, Remove, Remove'.
ERG colors: Yellow = Your number, Blue = By name, Orange = Orders (guide), Green = Gap (distances).
NFPA: Blue = Body (health), Red = Fire, Yellow = Yikes (unstable), White = Weird (special).
PPE: A = Airtight, B = Breathing (SCBA) but splash, C = Canister (filter), D = Daily uniform.

decisionTrees.title: Contaminated Casualty Flow
decisionTrees.content:
Suspected HazMat/chemical
  → Isolate, deny entry, upwind/uphill; ERG distances
  → Casualties: get ambulatory out of hot zone → instruct 'remove outer clothing'
  → Warm zone decon corridor (Level B/C teams):
       LSIs (airway, bleeding, antidote) by trained protected staff
       → Dry decon (default) | Wet decon (caustic, visible liquid, symptomatic)
  → Cold zone: triage/treat (EMS) → transport → notify hospital

references: NFPA 704 Standard System for the Identification of the Hazards of Materials
US HHS/BARDA PRISM — Primary Response Incident Scene Management guidance (mass decon)
